response.text: Schema validation only checks structural conformity (type, format, shape) of a value, not its semantic correctness or trustworthiness, so a well-formed payment destination can still be malicious, unauthorized, or unintended—validation must be paired with authorization, provenance checks, and business-logic verification to ensure actual safety.

Schema validation only checks structural conformance (type, format, shape), not semantic correctness—so a payment destination can be a syntactically valid identifier while still being fraudulent, unauthorized, or otherwise unintended by the user, meaning safety requires additional checks like authorization, provenance verification, and business-logic validation beyond mere schema conformance.

Schema validation only checks structural conformity (type, format, required fields), not semantic correctness, authorization, or intent, so a value can be perfectly well-formed—like a syntactically valid account or wallet address—while still being fraudulent, unauthorized, or simply the wrong recipient.

Schema validation only checks that a value has the correct type, format, or structure—it says nothing about whether that value is the *intended*, authorized, or non-malicious destination, so a well-formed account number or address could still be fraudulent, tampered with, or belong to an attacker.

Schema validation only checks a value's structural type/format (e.g., "is this a well-formed account number or address"), not its semantic correctness or trustworthiness—so a value can be perfectly well-formed yet still be attacker-controlled, mistyped, or otherwise pointing to the wrong recipient, meaning safety requires additional checks like authentication, authorization, and out-of-band verification of intent.

Schema validation only checks that a value has the correct type, format, or structure—it says nothing about whether that value is authorized, trusted, or the intended recipient, so an attacker-controlled but well-formed address (e.g., in a phishing or injection attack) can pass validation while still directing funds to the wrong destination.

Schema validation only checks structural conformance (type, format, shape), not semantic trustworthiness—so a syntactically valid account/address string could still be attacker-controlled, unauthorized, or mismatched with the intended recipient, requiring separate authentication and business-logic checks before it's safe to pay.

Schema validation only checks structural/type conformity (e.g., "is this a valid-looking account ID string"), not semantic correctness or authorization—so a value can be perfectly well-formed yet still be an attacker-controlled, mistyped, or otherwise unintended destination, meaning payment safety requires additional checks like business-logic validation, authorization verification, and out-of-band confirmation.

Schema validation only checks that a value has the right type, format, or structure—it says nothing about whether that value is the *correct, authorized, or unaltered* destination, so an attacker-controlled but well-formed account number or address will pass validation just as easily as a legitimate one.

Schema validation only confirms a value's type, format, or structure conforms to expected rules—it says nothing about whether the destination is authorized, uncompromised, or actually intended by the legitimate party, so an attacker-controlled but well-formed address can pass validation while still being unsafe.
